title: We built the same rifle three ways (generated, rebuilt in Blender by an agent, CAD by an agent + bake) and measured each one in Unreal
author: KovatiDev
selftext:
A generated mesh got us a playable rifle in one working session. It also arrived at the wrong size, with unreadable lettering, and the reload animation turned it ninety degrees. So we produced the same design through three pipelines for the same weapon skeleton and compared them.
    
    **1. Generated and rigged.** One concept drawing into Tripo. The segmented download was 92 pieces without UVs, on a different mesh from the textured one. A Blender script merged them into seven objects, baked the texture across and attached it to the skeleton. 10 thousand triangles. Fast, and wrong in four ways that gave no error.
    
    **2. Rebuilt in Blender by an agent.** Claude Code wrote and ran Blender Python, no manual modeling. Two early attempts failed: one recolored the generated mesh, the other invented a different rifle. What fixed it was a measurable gate: render the model as a flat mask from each drawing's camera, divide the shared area by the combined area, and allow no detail until the score reaches 0.95. Side views reached 0.96. Front and top never passed, because the drawings themselves did not agree with each other (they were generated as separate images). Result: 28 separate working parts, every one swept through its travel.
    
    **3. CAD in Plasticity, driven by an agent through MCP overnight, then baked.** 123 solids. 756 thousand triangles with attachments, 91 thousand after baking the detailed mesh onto a light one.
    
    Frame cost in first person, UE 5.8, budget 0.5 ms: straight from CAD 0.37 ms, as a Nanite skeletal mesh 0.63 ms (most of it ray tracing), baked 0.11 ms.
    
    What we would tell anyone starting: agents build accurately to a locked reference and invent features without one. Give them a number to hit, not a description. And a person still has to look: every design improvement in version 2 came from artist review of renders.
    
    Full write-up with all numbers on the Epic Developer Community: https://dev.epicgames.com/community/learning/tutorials/0RmDq/from-ai-generated-mesh-to-game-ready-asset-a-guide-for-unreal-engine-developers-artists
    
    It is one of ten guides I prepared in collaboration with Epic for their UE x AI use cases; four are live so far, and the series guide links them all: https://dev.epicgames.com/community/learning/tutorials/Jd2MJ/ai-assisted-game-production-in-unreal-engine-principles-method-and-a-guide-to-the-series
